title: The first census
unit: men twenty and older able to serve
summary: Numbered in the Wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the Exodus. Levi is left out (1:47–49), and Joseph is counted as two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, so there are still twelve. The twelve figures add up exactly to the 603,550 of 1:46, and the same total is given for the tabernacle's silver in Exodus 38:26. Every figure but Gad's (45,650) is a round hundred. How large the numbers are is debated: 'thousand' translates the Hebrew ʾeleph, which some scholars read here as a clan or military unit rather than a thousand.

sources.note: the same 603,550, each paying half a shekel

sources.title: 'The Census Lists of Numbers 1 and 26'
sources.author: George E. Mendenhall
sources.note: Journal of Biblical Literature 77, pp. 52–66; reads ʾeleph as a tribal subunit

sources.title: 'The Number of People in the Exodus from Egypt: Decoding Mathematically the Very Large Numbers in Numbers I and XXVI'

title: The second census
unit: men twenty and older able to serve
summary: Numbered on the plains of Moab at the end of the wilderness years: not one man from the first census was left except Caleb and Joshua (26:64–65). The total barely moves, 1,820 fewer than the 603,550 of Numbers 1, but the tribes do. Simeon falls by 37,100 to 22,200, from the third largest to the smallest; Manasseh grows by 20,500 and now comes before Ephraim, which fell by 8,000. The text does not say why Simeon shrank. The plague at Peor had just killed 24,000 (25:9) and the man at its centre was a Simeonite chief (25:14), and readers often connect the two, but that is an inference. The Levites are counted apart again, 23,000 males a month old or more (26:62).

sources.note: the Levites counted apart; none of the first census left but Caleb and Joshua
